hook: Your brain processes threat faster than you can consciously register it. By the time you know you're anxious, the anxiety has already started.
topic: The low road vs. high road — LeDoux's dual pathway model
body:
**There are two pathways your brain uses to process a potential threat.**

The fast one — what neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux called the low road — bypasses conscious thought entirely. It goes directly from the sensory input to the amygdala and triggers a stress response before your cortex has had time to evaluate whether the threat is real. You are already anxious before the part of your brain that thinks rationally has had any input.

The slow one — the high road — goes via the cortex. It evaluates, contextualises, reasons. But it arrives after the alarm has already sounded.

This is why knowing that a thought isn't rational doesn't make the feeling disappear. You're asking your rational mind to undo a process that didn't involve it. The feeling was generated before the reasoning started.

It also means this: the goal of intervention is not to reason your way out of the feeling. It's to give the nervous system a different signal once the alarm has sounded. Slow breathing works here — not because it changes the thought, but because it signals safety to the system that fired before your thinking mind arrived.

Different tool. Different target.
